title: When Validators Don’t Trigger: A Paired Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Repair for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N = 600 task pairs) to test whether a deterministic validator–guided repair pipeline (generate→validate→repair) reduces high‑risk semantic misconfigurations relative to single‑shot LLM generation in intent→vendor‑configuration tasks. The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one sampled initial candidate per pair was produced and reused by both arms; the guarded arm could differ from baseline only if the deterministic validator rejected that candidate and an automated repair executed. Using gpt-5-mini as the generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the validator, every shared initial candidate passed the validator in both baseline and guarded conditions (baseline = 600/600; guarded = 600/600). The paired absolute difference = 0.0 (95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). No automated repairs were invoked. We report the preregistered design, clarify the scientific meaning of shared_initial_candidate semantics and the archived model sampling record (temperature = null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling), present exact paired results, and discuss construct validity of validators, ceiling effects, and design implications for future generate→validate→repair evaluations.

sections.introduction: Intent‑driven NetOps systems translate operator intents into vendor‑specific device configurations. Prior prototype work demonstrates feasibility of LLM‑based intent→configuration translation and advocates validator‑ or tool‑augmentation (generate→validate→repair) to reduce LLM errors [1]–[3]. However, operationally meaningful evaluation gaps remain: how reliably do such pipelines prevent high‑risk semantic misconfigurations under adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents, and how should experiments be designed to measure the effects of validators and repairs? We preregistered and executed a narrowly scoped paired confirmatory study to answer the following question: Under shared_initial_candidate paired semantics (one sampled initial generation per task reused by both arms), does a deterministic validator‑guided repair pipeline reduce high‑risk semantic failures relative to accepting the single LLM generation? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment executed on 600 intent→configuration pairs with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null (ceiling) outcome that arises under shared_initial_candidate semantics; and (3) design recommendations for future evaluations that seek to measure validator/repair efficacy or generation‑level differences.
sections.related_work: Recent intent→configuration systems and case studies show that LLMs can produce usable vendor configurations for constrained datasets and testbeds, and multiple authors recommend augmenting generators with validators, retrieval, or deterministic checks to reduce errors [1], [2], [4]. Surveys of LLM hallucination, self‑correction, and agentic tool use document taxonomy, mitigation approaches (e.g., constrained decoding, neurosymbolic methods), and the benefits and limitations of tool augmentation across domains [3], [5], [6]. Importantly, prior work is heterogeneous in datasets, validator definitions, and evaluation metrics; it therefore motivates reproducible, workflow‑centered experiments that pair intents, vendor targets, deterministic validators, and adversarial/perturbed inputs—exactly the design decisions our preregistration aimed to make explicit.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as autocand-2026-01-prereg-v1 prior to observing outcomes. The confirmatory paired design used 600 deterministically selected task pairs (planned episodes = 1,200; complete pairs = 600). Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in high‑risk semantic failure proportions (guarded − baseline), tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as declared in the preregistration. Execution contract and generation semantics: per the preregistered adapter contract, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate: exactly one sampled initial generation per task was produced and reused unchanged by both baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded condition could call the validator and, if the deterministic validator failed, invoke at most one automated repair. Because of shared_initial_candidate semantics, the paired estimand measures whether the validator would have rejected the same initial candidate and whether a repair could convert that candidate into a validator‑passing configuration—it does not measure independent per‑condition generator variability. Models, adapter, and validators: the declared generator was gpt-5-mini. The deterministic validator used the full_intent_constraint_validation rule (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Tasks: synthetic intent→configuration tasks were produced by a deterministic task generator with workflow constraints and required sequences to create challenging, multi‑step maintenance changes. Sampling record and determinism statement: the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset for executed calls; null/unset is explicitly not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. All runtime sampling fields and provider traces are archived in the execution bundle (artifact manifest). Model‑call accounting clarification: the preregistered maximum_model_calls (1,200) represented the upper bound if independent per‑condition draws were performed; because shared_initial_candidate semantics used one initial generation per pair (shared by both arms), model_calls_used = 600 in the actual execution, consistent with the preregistered contract. Inclusion/exclusion and contamination controls: items lacking public provenance or failing automated provenance checks were excluded per the preregistered contamination plan. Analysis plan and power: the preregistration assumed a baseline high‑risk failure rate ≈10% to calibrate power to detect a 5 percentage‑point absolute difference (≈80% power). That assumption appears in the preregistration but the observed baseline rate differed (see Results). Reproducibility: preregistration identifier, execution manifest, raw results, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived as declared in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The adapter executed the preregistered paired run to completion with 600 completed pairs and no model‑call failures under the shared_initial_candidate contract. Primary outcomes: the deterministic validator accepted the shared initial candidate in every episode. Counts: baseline_success_count = 600/600 (100%), guarded_success_count = 600/600 (100%). Paired contingency: n11 = 600, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repairs invoked: none—no guarded repairs were executed because no validator failures occurred. Secondary preregistered estimands (vendor‑stratified differences, repair success rate, failure‑mode breakdown) are uninformative due to absence of failures; the archived analysis artifacts report the empty/fully passed summaries. Representative validator traces for several tasks are archived and show the validator's decision rationale and the shared_initial_candidate reuse.
sections.discussion: Scientific meaning of the null outcome: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded pipeline can alter a paired outcome only if the deterministic validator rejects the initial candidate and an automated repair produces a validator‑passing configuration. Because the validator accepted all initial candidates, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to demonstrate benefit; the observed null (ceiling) outcome therefore measures validator/repair trigger opportunities, not a generator‑level improvement. Design and interpretive implications: (1) Choose generation semantics to match the estimand: to measure generator‑level differences use independent per‑condition draws; to measure validator/repair trigger efficacy use shared_initial_candidate semantics. (2) Audit validators for construct validity (sensitivity/specificity) before confirmatory tests—overpermissive validators create ceiling effects that mask downstream protections. (3) Use adversarially stressed or harder task banks to avoid ceiling/floor effects and to elicit repair opportunities. Limitations and scope: tasks were synthetic and derived from the preregistered generator; only one generator (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; no independent seeded validator audit is reported among the archived confirmatory artifacts (a 100‑case seeded audit was preregistered but not executed as part of the confirmatory run), so validator sensitivity remains an unresolved limitation. The preregistered power assumptions (baseline ≈10%) do not hold for the observed baseline rate of 0%, so the planned minimal detectable effect interpretation does not apply here; instead we report exact paired results and discuss design lessons.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N = 600 pairs) under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing single‑shot LLM generation and a deterministic validator‑guided repair pipeline. Both arms passed the deterministic validator in all pairs (100% baseline and guarded success), producing an observed paired difference of 0.0 (95% CI [0.0, 0.0], p = 1.0). No automated repairs were invoked. This outcome highlights that (a) generation semantics determine what the paired estimand measures (validator trigger effectiveness vs. generation differences), (b) validators must be audited to avoid ceiling effects, and (c) future tests of generate→validate→repair benefits should use independent draws or intentionally harder/adversarial task banks to elicit validator failures. We archive preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts per the preregistered plan and provide concrete design recommendations for future evaluations.

disclosure_statement: Models, tools, and preregistration: generative calls used the declared model gpt-5-mini via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The deterministic validator implementation was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The study was preregistered as autocand-2026-01-prereg-v1 and executed under that preregistration. Autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and approved the initial master prompt before the autonomy lock; after the lock the AI system autonomously selected the final research question, executed the preregistered experiment, performed analyses, and drafted and revised the manuscript. No manual human editing of technical content, numerical results, or manuscript conclusions occurred after the autonomy lock. Master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Generation semantics and sampling: generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per pair was reused by baseline and guarded); the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset for the executed calls—null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The disclosure omits internal per‑file paths and per‑file hashes; full execution manifests, raw model calls, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived as declared in the preregistration and execution manifest.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: baseline and guarded used the identical sampled initial generation per pair; thus the paired estimand measures validator/repair trigger effectiveness, not independent generation differences.

Validator construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted all initial candidates in this run; without an independent validator sensitivity audit this ceiling performance limits inference about the utility of tool augmentation across other task banks.

Task external validity: tasks were synthetic items generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 under the preregistered contamination and redaction rules; results may not generalize to diverse production device configurations or vendor idiosyncrasies.
Model and adapter scope: only the declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one adapter/validator instance were used; no claim of model‑class generality is made.

Sampling record: the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is explicitly not evidence of deterministic sampling. Independent per‑condition sampling would be required to evaluate generator‑level effects.

Power assumptions violated: the preregistration's power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate (≈10%). The observed baseline rate was 0%, so the preregistered minimal detectable effect (5 percentage points) and power interpretation do not apply to this execution.

Planned validator audit not executed: a seeded 100‑case validator audit was preregistered but not executed as part of the archived confirmatory run; validator sensitivity therefore remains an unresolved limitation and a concrete recommendation for follow‑up work.
